title: Does Electoral Accountability Affect Economic Policy Choices? Evidence from Gubernatorial Term Limits
research_question: Do incentives created by re-election eligibility shape the economic policy choices made by elected executives? Specifically, when an executive can no longer stand for re-election, do tax and spending decisions differ systematically from those made when re-election is possible?
data_description: The analysis uses a state-level panel of U.S. states covering several decades in the post-war period. Key variables include state taxes (total taxes per capita and components such as sales, income, and corporate taxes), state government expenditures (total and by category, including welfare spending), and workers' compensation benefit levels. Political variables include the party of the sitting governor, whether the governor faces a binding term limit (i.e., is in a final term and ineligible to run again), and the partisan composition of the state legislature. Demographic and economic controls (income per capita, population, age structure, unemployment) are drawn from standard federal sources. The unit of observation is the state-year.
institutional_context: U.S. state governors operate under constitutional rules that vary across states and over time regarding how many consecutive terms they may serve. In some states governors face no limit; in others, they are restricted (most commonly to two consecutive terms), so that a sitting governor in his or her final allowable term cannot seek immediate re-election. This creates within-state, within-governor variation in whether the executive faces voters again. Because final-term governors no longer answer to an electoral sanction while otherwise retaining the same formal powers, the setting offers a sharp contrast between politicians who are accountable to voters and otherwise-similar politicians who are not, against the backdrop of state fiscal policymaking over taxes, spending, and social insurance programs.

_legacy_v1_ground_truth.identification_strategy: DID — treatment = term-limited governors, control = non-term-limited governors; shock/instrument/cutoff = term limit implementation

key_variables.control: Governors who are not term-limited and can seek re-election
key_variables.outcome: State fiscal policy measures (e.g., taxation, spending)
key_variables.time_period: Several decades covering multiple election cycles

_legacy_v1_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: Gubernatorial term limits lead to less fiscally responsible economic policy choices.
